rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sībawayh says assimilation and clear articulation vary in acceptability with articulatory similarity; clarity improves as points of articulation grow farther apart.
rows.anchor: المختلفة المخارج أحسن لأنها أشد تباعدا وكذلك الإظهار كلما تباعدت المخارج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hamza does not assimilate into a neighbor or receive assimilation, because its characteristic heaviness is handled by alteration or deletion.
rows.anchor: لأنها إنما أمرها في الاستثقال التغيير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alif does not assimilate even with a neighboring alif: doing so would change both long vowels into other sounds, so it also resists nearby consonants.
rows.anchor: وكذلك الألف لا تدغم في الهاء ولا فيما تقاربه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Long yāʾ or wāw after fatḥa resist assimilation into adjacent consonants, because this would turn a sound with length and softness into one without them.
rows.anchor: لأن فيهما لينا ومدا فلم تقو عليهما الجيم والباء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A following consonant cannot assimilate into a long yāʾ, since that would introduce softness into a sound that lacks it.
rows.anchor: فلا تدخل ما لا يكون فيه اللين على ما يكون فيه اللين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mīm does not assimilate into bāʾ: when nūn changes before bāʾ, speakers choose mīm, so mīm is already the sound they turn to.
rows.anchor: فالميم لا تدغم في الباء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fāʾ does not assimilate into bāʾ because of their articulation; bāʾ can assimilate into fāʾ through proximity and oral-consonant assimilation.
rows.anchor: والفاء لا تدغم في الباء لأنها من باطن الشفة السفلى وأطراف ~~الثنايا العلى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāʾ resists assimilation into lām or nūn because its trill and spread would be impaired; lām and nūn may assimilate into rāʾ without that loss.
rows.anchor: والراء لا تدغم في اللام ولا في النون ~~لأنها مكررة وهي تفشى إذا كان معها غيرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shīn does not assimilate into jīm because its extended, diffuse articulation makes the change objectionable; jīm may assimilate into shīn.
rows.anchor: والشين لا تدغم في الجيم لأن الشين استطال مخرجها لرخاوتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With hāʾ and ḥāʾ, clear articulation is preferable, though assimilation is good because the two are close and share voiceless softness.
rows.anchor: اجبه حملا البيان أحسن لاختلاف المخرجين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For ʿayn followed by hāʾ, clarity is preferable; assimilation is possible after changing the adjacent sounds to ḥāʾ, so assimilation occurs between like sounds.
rows.anchor: كقولك اقطع هلالا البيان أحسن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With ʿayn and ḥāʾ, both clear articulation and assimilation are good because they share a point of articulation.
rows.anchor: كقولك اقطع حملا الإدغام حسن والبيان حسن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For ghayn and khāʾ, clarity is preferable though assimilation is acceptable; in the reverse order, clarity is better because ghayn is voiced.
rows.anchor: الغين مع الخاء ~~البيان أحسن والإدغام حسن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With qāf and kāf, both assimilation and clarity are good; clarity is preferable for kāf before qāf because these are the tongue consonants nearest the throat.
rows.anchor: الإدغام حسن والبيان حسن وإنما أدغمت لقرب المخرجين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jīm and shīn may be either assimilated or articulated clearly because they share the middle-tongue articulation point.
rows.anchor: الجيم مع الشين كقولك ~~ابعج شيئا الإدغام والبيان حسنان لأنهما من مخرج واحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lām assimilates into rāʾ most naturally: their articulation points are close and both share a lateral quality.
rows.anchor: اللام مع الراء نحو اشغل رحبة لقرب المخرجين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nūn assimilates into rāʾ, with or without nasalization, because their articulation points are close and both are tongue consonants.
rows.anchor: النون تدغم مع الراء لقرب المخرجين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nūn assimilates into lām either with nasalization retained or without it; keeping nasalization preserves nūn's nasal sound.
rows.anchor: وتدغم في اللام لأنها قريبة منها على طرف اللسان وذلك قولك من لك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nūn assimilates into mīm because their sounds are alike and both are voiced; their shared nasal resonance outweighs their different articulation points.
rows.anchor: وتدغم النون مع الميم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Before bāʾ, nūn changes to mīm rather than bāʾ: mīm shares nūn's sound and bāʾ's articulation place, while bāʾ lacks nasal resonance.
rows.anchor: وتقلب النون مع الباء ميما لأنها من موضع تعتل فيه النون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nūn assimilates into wāw with or without nasalization, but does not become mīm because wāw is a soft, extended sound unlike mīm.
rows.anchor: كرهوا أن يكون مكانها أشبه الحروف من موضع الواو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nūn assimilates into yāʾ with or without nasalization: yāʾ resembles wāw and is close to rāʾ, which itself is close to nūn.
rows.anchor: وتدغم النون مع الياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Before other oral consonants, nūn may be a hidden sound articulated through the nose; this is lighter and remains identifiable because no other sound comes from that place.
rows.anchor: وكان العلم بها أنها نون من ذلك الموضع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When nūn is assimilated with nasalization into rāʾ, lām, yāʾ, or wāw, its articulation stays oral and only takes on nasal resonance.
rows.anchor: ولكن صوت الفم أشرب غنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nūn remains clearly articulated before hamza and the five throat consonants because they are distant from it and do not belong to its articulation class.
rows.anchor: وتكون مع الهمزة والهاء والعين والحاء والغين والخاء بينة موضعها من الفم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A hidden nūn does not assimilate into following throat consonants, nor do they become nūn, because they are distant and unlike it.
rows.anchor: ولم تقرب قرب هذه الستة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When nūn and mīm occur within one word, they are clearly distinguished, as are nūn before wāw and yāʾ, to avoid confusion with a geminate form.
rows.anchor: والواو والياء بمنزلتها مع حروف الحلق

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl analyzes the derived form from wajila as awjal, by analogy with amḥā, because the added nūn occurs in a pattern without a doubled wāw.
rows.anchor: وسمعت الخليل يقول في انفعل من وجلت اوجل كما قالوا امحى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nūn before rāʾ or lām is not normally left clear because the nearby articulation makes clarity heavy; assimilation risks confusion with genuine gemination.
rows.anchor: ولم يجز فيه ما جاز في ود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Definite-article lām must assimilate before thirteen consonants, including ṭāʾ; this rule accounts for the assimilated lām in al-muṭallaqāt.
rows.anchor: هذه الحروف أحد عشر حرفا منها حروف طرف اللسان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The article lām's obligatory assimilation set comprises eleven tongue-tip consonants plus ḍād and shīn, whose articulation extends toward neighboring places.
rows.anchor: والشين كذلك حتى اتصلت بمخرج الطاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With lām outside the definite article, assimilation into rāʾ is preferable because rāʾ is closest and most similar; clear articulation remains valid in Hijazi speech.
rows.anchor: فإذا كانت غير لام المعرفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Assimilation of non-article lām into ṭāʾ, dāl, tāʾ, ṣād, zāy, or sīn is allowed but less natural than before rāʾ because these sounds are farther away.
rows.anchor: وهن من الثنايا وليس منهن انحراف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lām assimilation into ẓāʾ, thāʾ, or dhāl is allowed but weaker; it is weaker still with ḍād and shīn, though connected articulation permits it.
rows.anchor: وهن من حروف طرف اللسان كما أنهن منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭarīf's verse attests to non-article lām assimilating into shīn, producing hīshiʾ for hal shayʾ.
rows.anchor: فكيهة هشيء بكفيك لائق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū ʿAmr read hal thūb al-kuffār with lām assimilated into thāʾ, yielding hathūb.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو عمرو ^ ( هثوب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A reading assimilates the lām of bal into tāʾ in bal tuʾthirūna al-ḥayāta al-dunyā, yielding batūthirūna.
rows.anchor: وقد قرئ بها ^ ( بتؤثرون الحياة الدنيا ) ^ فأدغم اللام في التاء

rows.speaker: مزاحم العقيلي
rows.claim: Muzāḥim al-ʿUqaylī's verse witnesses lām assimilated into tāʾ, giving hataʿīn for hal taʿīn.
rows.anchor: وقال مزاحم العقيلي # % فدع ذا ولكن هتعين متيما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nūn is the least suitable target for lām assimilation, since nūn assimilates into lām and several other consonants, making the reverse pattern awkward.
rows.anchor: والنون إدغامها في أقبح من جميع هذه الحروف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Frequently used demonstratives and indeclinable expressions change when made proper names; Sībawayh attributes this treatment to Yūnus, al-Khalīl, and other grammarians.
rows.anchor: تقع على كل شيء وكثرت في كلامهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The demonstrative ذا remains masculine when used as a name, except that ʿĪsā reportedly declined it for a woman named ʿAmr.
rows.anchor: ذا اسم مؤنث لأنه مذكر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As proper names, ذي behaves like في and تا behaves like لا.
rows.anchor: وأما ذي فبمنزلة في وتا بمنزلة لا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ألاء is fully declinable as a man's name; ألا takes tanwīn like هدى because it is not derived or altered, and its plural-relative use also follows هدى.
rows.anchor: ألا ليس بمشتق ولا معدولا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If الذي or التي is used as a proper name, remove the article because it names the person; if it remains a relative pronoun, retain its relative clause and inflect it like عم.
rows.anchor: أخرجت الألف واللام لأنك تجعله علما له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: اللائي and اللاتي behave like شائي and ضاري: the article is removed, and retaining or deleting yāʾ determines the declensional pattern.
rows.anchor: وأما ألائي واللاتي فبمنزلة شائي وضاري وتخرج منه الألف واللام

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl says ذين used as a man's name remains in its dual form because the name is not impaired by that shape.
rows.anchor: عن ذين اسم رجل فقال هو بمنزلة رجلين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Names derived from أولو or ذوو take the forms ألون and ذوون when not annexed; Sībawayh cites Qur'an 27:33 and al-Kumayt's الذوينا as evidence.
rows.anchor: وإنما ذهبت النون في الإضافة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ذو مال and ذو يزن remain unchanged as names because annexation makes the genitive element the name's ending and removes tanwīn, like أبو زيد.
rows.anchor: قالوا ذو يزن منصرف فلم يغيروه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: أمس as a proper name is declinable because it is no longer an adverb; its ordinary adverbial form is fixed like أين and غاق.
rows.anchor: وسألته عن أمس اسم رجل فقال مصروف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sībawayh reports that Hijaz keeps أمس in the genitive form throughout; Tamim leaves its nominative indeclinable because this form departs from ordinary usage, like أخر and temporal سحر.
rows.anchor: فلما عدلوه عن أصله في الكلام ومجراه تركوا صرفه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If أمس is made a personal name in the Tamimi dialect, it is declinable in every case because it already declines in the oblique cases.
rows.anchor: في هذا القول صرفته لأنك لا بد لك من أن تصرفه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: سحر used as a man's name is declinable, especially because a proper name does not function as an adverb; if it did, its case behavior would parallel أمس.
rows.anchor: وكذلك سحر اسم رجل تصرفه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some speakers opened the final vowel of أمس after مذ when using it for a past day; Sībawayh calls this rare and cites a poem.
rows.anchor: لقد رأيت عجبا مذ أمسا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ذه as a proper name has hāʾ replacing the yāʾ found in ذي; the extra yāʾ in ذهي is only a clarifying glide before the hāʾ.
rows.anchor: وأما ذه اسم رجل فإنك تقول هذا ذه قد جاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Speakers who say ذهي أمة الله omit the clarifying yāʾ when pausing; Sībawayh also heard eloquent Arabs use ذه and sometimes leave its hāʾ unvocalized in connected speech.
rows.anchor: فيسكنون الهاء في الوصل كما يقولون بهم
